IRD29 · Microbiology · Study Guide

Viral Exanthems

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Sort skin eruptions into the two big rash patterns (scarlatiniform vs morbilliform), name what causes each, and recognize the features all the childhood viral rashes share.
  2. LO 2Walk through how measles, rubella, chickenpox (and its comeback as shingles), parvovirus B19, roseola and mumps present: prodrome, rash course, who gets sick and what can go wrong.
  3. LO 3Explain how enteroviruses (echo- and coxsackieviruses) show up on the skin, with hand-foot-and-mouth disease from coxsackie A16 as the must-know example.
  4. LO 4Recognize scarlet fever (a bacterial toxin rash) and tell it apart from its strawberry-tongue look-alike, Kawasaki disease.
  5. LO 5Pick out the key exanthems on darker skin, where redness is subtle and texture, distribution and associated signs carry the diagnosis.

MAPBig picture

  • Exanthem = acute generalized skin eruption → 2 looks
    • Scarlatiniform → confluent blanching “sunburn” → scarlet fever · TSS · Kawasaki · drug
    • Morbilliform → discrete macules/papules → measles · rubella · roseola · fifth · drug
  • Childhood viral rashes → airborne/droplet · shed in oropharynx · outbreaks · worse in adults · fetal harm
  • Timing is the tiebreaker
    • Measles → 3 C's + Koplik → rash head → toe · contagious 5 d before → 4 d after rash
    • Roseola → 3–4 d high fever → rash as fever breaks
    • Varicella → crops on trunk → asynchronous stages
  • Signature complications
    • Measles → giant cell pneumonitis · encephalitis
    • Rubella → arthritis · ↓ platelets · congenital deafness/heart/ID
    • B19 → small-joint arthritis · aplastic crisis · hydrops
    • Mumps → orchitis · pancreatitis · CNS
    • VZV → superinfection (GAS, S. aureus) · zoster (PHN, Hutchinson, Ramsay Hunt)
  • Enteroviruses → many rash types → must-know = coxsackie A16 → HFM (kids <10, summer/fall)
  • Strawberry tongue → scarlet fever (GAS toxin → penicillin) vs Kawasaki (vasculitis → IVIG + aspirin)
  • Darker skin → redness hides → read texture · distribution · lesion type · mucosa

LO 1Rash vocabulary and the two exanthem typesScarlatiniform vs morbilliform, plus what the childhood viral rashes have in common

By the end: you can define exanthem, describe and give examples of each rash type, list the six shared features of childhood viral exanthems, and use the master table to match every disease to its virus, rash, complication and risk group.
Q1. What is an exanthem, and what words do we use to describe a rash?
  • Exanthem = an acute, generalized eruption of the skin, usually riding along with a systemic (often viral) infection.
    • Enanthem = the same idea on a mucous membrane → e.g., Koplik spots (measles), Forchheimer spots (rubella), oral vesicles of HFM.
  • Lesion words you need:
    • Macule = flat color change · papule = small raised bump · vesicle = small fluid-filled blister · crust = dried exudate.
    • Confluent = lesions merge into sheets · blanching = redness disappears with pressure (blood is in dilated vessels, not leaked out).
    • Petechiae/purpura = non-blanching (blood outside vessels) → think meningococcemia, low platelets, some enteroviruses.
CheckYou press a clear drinking glass against a red rash and it turns white. Blanching or non-blanching, and what does that tell you?
Blanching → the red is from dilated capillaries (erythema), not extravasated blood. Typical of viral exanthems and scarlet fever; non-blanching would push you toward petechiae/purpura.
Q2. What are the two exanthem types, and which diseases go in each bucket?

Scarlatiniform

  • Confluent, diffuse, blanching erythema → looks like a sunburn
  • Causes: scarlet fever, toxic shock syndrome, Kawasaki disease, drug eruption
  • Mostly toxin- or immune-driven, not viral

Morbilliform (“measles-like”)

  • Discrete erythematous macules and papules (may merge later)
  • Causes: rubeola (measles), rubella, roseola, erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), drug eruption
  • The classic childhood viral exanthems
CheckWhich single cause appears in BOTH the scarlatiniform and morbilliform lists?
Drug eruption. Always ask about new medications for any generalized rash.
Memory tool

“Morbilli” = Latin for measles → morbilliform literally means “looks like measles.” Scarlatiniform = “looks like scarlet fever” → a red sunburn sheet.

Step 1 trap

Not every rash in this topic is viral: scarlet fever is bacterial (group A strep toxin), Kawasaki is a vasculitis, TSS is a superantigen toxin disease. A “viral exanthem” question can still have a bacterial answer.

Q3. What do the classic childhood viral exanthems have in common?
SpreadHighly infectious by the airborne / respiratory droplet route
→
ShedVirus shed in oropharyngeal secretions
→
WhoExposure + infection in childhood; epidemics/outbreaks are common
→
DangerAdults get sicker; pregnancy infection can harm the fetus
  • Fetal examples to have ready: congenital rubella, parvovirus B19 → hydrops fetalis, congenital varicella.
  • Adult examples: varicella pneumonia (adults), rubella arthritis (adults), B19 arthropathy (adults), mumps orchitis (post-pubertal).
CheckWhy do these viruses cause such big outbreaks?
They spread by the respiratory route, are shed before or around symptom onset (measles is contagious 5 days before the rash), and mostly infect susceptible children in close-contact settings, so one case seeds many.

CheckWhich agent in the table is the only single-stranded DNA virus?
Parvovirus B19. VZV and HHV-6 are dsDNA herpesviruses; measles, mumps, rubella and coxsackie are RNA viruses.
Step 1 HY
  • MMR = live attenuated vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella; varicella also has a live attenuated vaccine (avoid live vaccines in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression).
  • Boards list rubella virus as a matonavirus (formerly togavirus). Same disease, new family name.
  • Numbered diseases: 1st measles, 2nd scarlet fever, 3rd rubella, 4th (historic), 5th = erythema infectiosum, 6th = roseola.
Step 1 trap

Paramyxovirus = measles + mumps (and RSV, parainfluenza). Rubella is not a paramyxovirus, even though it sits in MMR. Don't let the vaccine grouping set the family.

Buzzwords
"sunburn-like, blanching, confluent" → scarlatiniform"discrete macules and papules" → morbilliform"acute generalized eruption" → exanthem"lesions on mucosa" → enanthem

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1A 5-year-old has a diffuse red rash that feels like fine sandpaper and merges into one sheet over the trunk. Which exanthem type, and what is the most likely cause?
Scarlatiniform → scarlet fever. Confluent, blanching, sandpaper-textured erythema is the textbook scarlatiniform pattern; ask about recent sore throat.
A2A pregnant teacher asks why the school's rash outbreak matters more to her than to the children. What two general principles apply?
Adult infections are more severe, and infection in pregnancy can harm the fetus (e.g., rubella → congenital defects; B19 → hydrops fetalis; VZV → congenital varicella).
A3A rash is described as “discrete erythematous macules and papules.” Name four infectious diseases and one non-infectious cause that fit.
Measles, rubella, roseola, erythema infectiosum (fifth) + drug eruption. That is the morbilliform list.
A4A child's rash does not blanch and looks like tiny purple dots. Why should this change your thinking away from a “routine” viral exanthem?
Non-blanching petechiae/purpura = blood outside vessels. Think meningococcemia, thrombocytopenia (e.g., rubella can lower platelets) or petechial enterovirus rashes (echovirus 9). These need urgent evaluation.

LO 2The classic six: measles, rubella, VZV, parvovirus B19, roseola, mumpsProdrome → rash course → complications for each

By the end: for each of the six you can give the virus family, how it spreads, the prodrome, the rash start and spread, the risk group and the signature complications, and you can use rash timing and distribution to separate them.
Q1. How do timing and distribution separate the rashes before you even look closely?

Two questions crack most exanthem vignettes: (1) how does the rash relate to the fever/prodrome? and (2) where does it start and which way does it spread?

Where does it start?

CheckTwo febrile toddlers: one gets a rash while still febrile and coughing, the other gets a rash the morning the fever finally breaks. Which is which?
Rash with ongoing fever + cough/coryza/conjunctivitis → measles. Rash appearing as the fever breaks → roseola (HHV-6).
Memory tool
  • Measles = “top-down”: starts at the hairline/face and pours down like a bucket of red paint.
  • Roseola: fever first, rosy (rash) later.
  • Varicella = a “starry sky”: new and old lesions twinkling at different stages.
Q2. Measles (rubeola): what is the full story from exposure to complication?
ExposureRespiratory droplets; 90% attack rate in the susceptible; incubation 6–19 d (median 13)
→
ProdromeFever + cough, coryza, conjunctivitis
→
EnanthemKoplik spots: blue-gray spots on buccal mucosa opposite the 2nd molars
→
ExanthemBright red maculopapular, face → trunk → extremities, becomes confluent, can blanch; 7–10 d
  • Virus: paramyxovirus, single-stranded RNA.
  • Contagious from 5 days BEFORE the rash until 4 days AFTER → patients spread it during the prodrome, before anyone suspects measles → outbreaks.
  • Rash rarely involves palms and soles.
  • Complications: giant cell pneumonitis and encephalitis.
  • Epidemiology: U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000, but cases keep coming through importation into pockets of unvaccinated people:
    • 2011: 222 cases → ~90% linked to importation; 86% unvaccinated or unknown status.
    • 2014–2015: multistate outbreak starting in California (an amusement-park outbreak) from an imported strain.
    • Recent surge (2025, largest in the Southwest) → linked to falling childhood vaccination.
CheckAn unvaccinated boy's measles rash appeared on Thursday. His sister played with him on Wednesday. Was she exposed?
Yes. Measles is contagious from 5 days before the rash, so Wednesday (1 day before) is well within the window.
Step 1 HY
  • SSPE (subacute sclerosing panencephalitis) = fatal late complication years after measles.
  • Pneumonia is the most common cause of measles death in children; vitamin A lowers morbidity/mortality.
  • Lymphoid tissue: Warthin-Finkeldey multinucleated giant cells (F protein → cell fusion).
  • Post-exposure: MMR within 72 h or immune globulin within 6 d for susceptible contacts.
Memory tool

4 C's of measles: Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis, “C”oplik spots. The rash follows the C's.

Buzzwords
"blue-gray spots opposite 2nd molars" → Koplik → measles"rash starts at hairline, spreads down" → measles"unvaccinated, recent international travel" → measles"giant cell pneumonia" → measles
Q3. Rubella: how is it like measles, how is it different, and why does pregnancy matter?
  • Virus: togavirus, ssRNA. Eliminated from the U.S. since 2004; most common in children 5–9 y; spread by respiratory droplets.
  • Postnatal rubella (mild illness):
    • Posterior cervical, posterior auricular and posterior occipital lymphadenopathy ← the clue.
    • Maculopapular rash on the face → spreads to trunk; similar distribution to measles but less intensely red; can desquamate.
    • Forchheimer spots = petechiae on the soft palate.
  • Complications: arthritis (fingers, wrists, knees, mainly adults) and thrombocytopenia.
  • Congenital rubella (mother infected in pregnancy, highest risk in 1st trimester) → deafness, congenital heart disease, intellectual disability.
FeatureMeaslesRubella
FamilyParamyxovirusTogavirus
How sickQuite ill; striking prodromeMild, often barely ill
ProdromeFever + 3 C'sLow-grade; tender posterior nodes
EnanthemKoplik spots (buccal)Forchheimer spots (soft palate petechiae)
RashBright red, face → down, confluent, 7–10 dPink, face → trunk, fainter, short
Big complicationGiant cell pneumonitis, encephalitisArthritis, low platelets, congenital rubella
CheckA mildly ill 8-year-old has a fading pink facial rash and tender nodes behind the ears and at the base of the skull, without cough or conjunctivitis. Measles or rubella?
Rubella. Mild illness, fainter rash and posterior auricular/occipital nodes; measles would bring the 3 C's, Koplik spots and a brighter, confluent rash.
Step 1 HY
  • Congenital rubella classic triad: cataracts, sensorineural deafness, PDA (heart) ± “blueberry muffin” rash (dermal extramedullary hematopoiesis).
  • Rubella is a member of TORCH; boards now call it a matonavirus.
Memory tool

“I ♥ ruby earrings” → eye (cataracts), heart (PDA), ears (deafness) for congenital rubella. Rubella's nodes are in the back (posterior cervical, auricular, occipital).

Step 1 trap

Rubella and measles spread the same direction (face → down), so direction alone won't separate them. Use severity, posterior nodes and the enanthem (Koplik vs Forchheimer).

Q4. Varicella (chickenpox): how does the rash evolve, and what goes wrong?
  • Virus: varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a herpesvirus, dsDNA. Incubation 14–21 d.
  • Fever + an itchy (pruritic) vesicular rash.
Maculeflat red spot
→
Papuleraised bump
→
Vesicleclear blister on red base
→
Crustscab
  • Lesions appear in crops, starting on the trunk, and are asynchronous → macules, papules, vesicles and crusts all present at the same time.
  • Complications:
    • Encephalitis, pneumonitis (worse in adults: patchy perihilar interstitial infiltrates), hepatitis.
    • Bacterial superinfection of scratched lesions by group A Streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus (impetigo, cellulitis, invasive GAS).
    • Later in life → herpes zoster (shingles).
CheckFour days into chickenpox, one lesion on a child's thigh becomes a hot, spreading, tender red plaque with new high fever. What happened?
Bacterial superinfection of a varicella lesion by group A strep or S. aureus (cellulitis).
Step 1 HY
  • Tzanck smear → multinucleated giant cells in HSV and VZV (outdated; PCR preferred).
  • No aspirin in children with varicella (or influenza) → Reye syndrome.
  • Varicella vaccine = live attenuated.
Step 1 trap

Asynchronous lesions = varicella. Smallpox lesions are all in the same stage and concentrated on the face/extremities. Don't swap them.

Buzzwords
"dew drops on a rose petal" → varicella vesicle"lesions in different stages" → varicella"crops on the trunk, itchy" → varicella
Q5. Herpes zoster (shingles): where does VZV hide, and what are the special forms?
  • Herpes zoster = reactivation of latent VZV from sensory nerve ganglia (dorsal root ganglia for the body; cranial ganglia such as trigeminal and geniculate for the head).
  • Most common in the elderly and immunocompromised.
  • Can begin with a prodrome of localized pain (in the area where the rash will appear) → crops of vesicles in a dermatomal distribution; thoracic/lumbar most common.
  • Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN): pain persisting in the dermatome after healing, 3–4 months (or longer); the most common complication.
  • Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve; Hutchinson sign = vesicle on the tip of the nose (nasociliary involvement) → eye at risk.
  • Ramsay Hunt syndrome: ear pain, vesicles within the auditory canal, ipsilateral facial palsy, loss of taste.
CheckA zoster patient has vesicles on the forehead and one on the tip of the nose. Which nerve branch, and why the urgency?
V1 (ophthalmic) → nasociliary branch. The nasociliary nerve also supplies the eye, so a nose-tip vesicle (Hutchinson sign) predicts ocular involvement → urgent eye evaluation.
Step 1 HY
  • Treat zoster early with acyclovir / valacyclovir / famciclovir; PHN → gabapentin, pregabalin, TCAs.
  • Recombinant zoster vaccine for adults ≥50.
  • Zoster in a young adult or multi-dermatomal/disseminated zoster → look for immunosuppression (offer HIV testing).
Memory tool

Ramsay Hunt = “Bell palsy + ear blisters.” Hutchinson sign: “the nose knows about the eye.”

Step 1 trap

An idiopathic Bell palsy has no vesicles. Facial palsy with ear-canal vesicles and ear pain = VZV (Ramsay Hunt), not idiopathic Bell palsy.

Q6. Parvovirus B19: why does one virus cause a cute cheek rash in kids and a crisis in sickle cell disease?
  • Virus: erythrovirus, single-stranded DNA. ~80% of adults have B19 antibodies (most infected as kids).
  • Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease): prodrome of fever, headache, coryza, diarrhea → “slapped cheek” fiery red facial rash with circumoral pallor (spares nasolabial folds) → may also see rash on the trunk.
  • B19 infects and lyses erythroid progenitors → RBC production stops briefly. Whether that matters depends on the host:
CheckWhy does a 1-week pause in RBC production go unnoticed in a healthy child but cause severe anemia in sickle cell disease?
Normal RBCs live ~120 days, so a week without new cells barely dents Hb. Sickle RBCs live only ~10–20 days, so a week-long stop → Hb crashes with reticulocytes near 0 = transient aplastic crisis.
Step 1 HY
  • Receptor = P antigen (globoside) on erythroid cells; marrow shows giant pronormoblasts.
  • Parvovirus = the only ssDNA virus that infects humans and is naked.
  • By the time the slapped-cheek rash appears, the child is no longer contagious (rash is immune-complex mediated) → no need to exclude from school.
Step 1 trap

Adult with symmetric small-joint arthritis of hands/wrists after contact with kids → B19 arthropathy, not early rheumatoid arthritis. Ask about a “slapped cheek” child at home or school.

Buzzwords
"slapped cheek, circumoral pallor" → B19"lacy reticular rash on trunk/limbs" → B19"sickle cell + reticulocytes ~0" → aplastic crisis (B19)"hydrops fetalis" → B19
Q7. Roseola infantum: what is the one sequence you must remember?
  • Virus: HHV-6 (dsDNA herpesvirus); exanthem subitum can also come from HHV-7.
  • Age: 6 months – 4 years.
  • Usually presents as high fever → can cause febrile seizures in young children.
Days 1–4High fever for 3–4 days; child often looks surprisingly well; ± febrile seizure
→
DefervescenceFever breaks
→
RashAt the time the fever fades: maculopapular rash on neck and trunk, pale pink almond-shaped macules
  • May also see cough and lymphadenopathy.
CheckA parent says, “Her fever finally broke this morning, and now she has a rash. Is she getting worse?” What do you tell them?
Classic roseola (HHV-6): the rash appearing as the fever fades is the expected end of the illness, not a worsening.
Memory tool

Roseola: fever first, rosy rash later. “Sixth disease” → HHV-6.

Step 1 trap

Toddler with febrile seizure + high fever and no focus → think roseola before meningitis if the child is well between spikes and later develops the rash. Rash with fever = measles; rash after fever = roseola.

Q8. Mumps: no skin rash, so why is it here, and what are its complications?
  • Virus: paramyxovirus, ssRNA; spread by respiratory droplets; incubation 16–18 d. It belongs with the classic childhood respiratory viruses and the MMR vaccine.
  • Clinical: low-grade fever, headache, parotitis (swelling obscuring the angle of the jaw) ± other salivary glands.
  • Complications (inflammation of glands and reproductive organs):
    • Epididymo-orchitis in 20–30% of post-pubescent males.
    • Oophoritis.
    • Pancreatitis.
    • CNS: CSF pleocytosis in ~51%, ~10% meningoencephalitis.
  • Prevention: MMR, two doses ≈ 88% effective (range 66–95%) → protection is incomplete, so outbreaks still happen in vaccinated groups.
  • Who gets it in outbreaks: school-aged children and college students / young adults in close contact:
    • 2006 U.S. outbreak: 6,584 cases centered in Iowa; highest attack rate at 18–24 y (mostly college students); only 13% unvaccinated.
    • Later: university and pro-hockey outbreaks; 2016–2017 Arkansas (~3,000 cases, mostly school-aged children).
CheckWhy can a college student who had both MMR doses still get mumps?
Two-dose MMR is only ~88% effective against mumps (and immunity can wane), so in crowded dorms with intense exposure, vaccinated people can still be infected.
Step 1 HY
  • Post-pubertal orchitis can cause subfertility/sterility (rarely complete).
  • Parotitis/pancreatitis → ↑ serum amylase.
  • Mumps is a common cause of aseptic (viral) meningitis in the unvaccinated.
Memory tool

POM-Poms: Parotitis, Orchitis (and oophoritis), Meningitis/encephalitis, Pancreatitis.

Buzzwords
"swelling obscures angle of jaw" → parotitis → mumps"college outbreak, vaccinated students" → mumps"testicular pain a week after parotitis" → mumps orchitis

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A malnourished, unvaccinated 3-year-old with measles becomes tachypneic and hypoxemic 5 days into the rash, then confused. Which two classic complications fit?
Giant cell pneumonitis and measles encephalitis. These are the two named complications of measles; vitamin A is the Step 1 add-on.
A2A 9-year-old with sickle cell disease has Hb fall from 8 to 4 g/dL with reticulocytes near 0; his brother has red cheeks. Diagnosis?
Parvovirus B19 transient aplastic crisis. B19 halts erythropoiesis; with short RBC survival, Hb collapses.
A3A 68-year-old on chemotherapy has right ear pain, vesicles in the right ear canal, cannot close his right eye and food tastes bland. Diagnosis and site of reactivation?
Ramsay Hunt syndrome: VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of CN VII (ear pain + canal vesicles + ipsilateral facial palsy + taste loss).
A4A woman with no vaccine record has a mild facial rash, postauricular nodes and finger joint pain at 9 weeks of pregnancy. What fetal outcomes worry you?
Congenital rubella: deafness, congenital heart disease (PDA), intellectual disability (plus cataracts); first-trimester infection carries the highest risk.
A5A 20-year-old with two MMR doses gets bilateral jaw-angle swelling during a campus outbreak, then a painful swollen testis a week later. Diagnosis and complication?
Mumps → epididymo-orchitis (20–30% of post-pubescent males). Two-dose MMR is only ~88% effective.

LO 3Enteroviruses and hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseEcho- and coxsackieviruses can mimic almost any rash; coxsackie A16 is the one to know cold

By the end: you can name the four enterovirus rash patterns with an example each, and fully describe hand-foot-and-mouth disease: cause, age, season, oral and skin findings, and its look-alike.
Q1. What rash patterns can enteroviruses (echovirus and coxsackievirus) produce?

Enteroviruses are rash chameleons: they can copy every other pattern in this topic. Know the categories; know the details only for coxsackie A16.

Rash patternWhat it looks likeExample enteroviruses
Rubelliform / morbilliformMaculopapular eruption (like rubella/measles)Echovirus 9
RoseoliformRash begins when fever subsides (like roseola)Echovirus 16; coxsackie B1, B5; echo 11, 25
HerpetiformVesicular rashCoxsackie A16 (HFM); other coxsackie/echoviruses; enterovirus 71
Petechial / purpuricNon-blanching spotsEchovirus 9; coxsackievirus 9
CheckA febrile child has a petechial rash during a summer echovirus outbreak. Why can't you simply reassure the family?
A petechial rash (echovirus 9) mimics meningococcemia, which is life-threatening, so it must be excluded first.
Step 1 HY
  • Enteroviruses = picornaviruses: (+)ssRNA, naked, fecal-oral (and respiratory) spread, summer/fall.
  • Other enterovirus syndromes: aseptic meningitis (most common cause), herpangina (coxsackie A: posterior pharynx vesicles), myocarditis/pericarditis and pleurodynia (coxsackie B).
Memory tool

Coxsackie A → Above the neck and skin (HFM, herpangina); Coxsackie B → Body organs (heart = myocarditis, pleura).

Q2. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFM): how do you recognize it?

Cause

Coxsackievirus A16 (most common); also other enteroviruses (e.g., enterovirus 71).

Who / when

Children <10 years; seasonal, mostly summer and fall.

Mouth

Sore throat, difficulty eating; vesicles on buccal mucosa and tongue → aphthae-like erosions anywhere in the mouth.

Hands + feet

Painful papulovesicular lesions on the hands and feet: pale white oval vesicles with a red rim.

  • One phrase: “vesicular stomatitis with exanthem.”
  • HFM lesions look similar to HSV → the distribution (mouth + hands + feet) and age/season give it away.
CheckA 3-year-old in August refuses to eat because of mouth sores; two days later small blisters appear on the hands and feet. Most likely virus?
Coxsackievirus A16 → hand-foot-and-mouth disease.
Step 1 HY

Boards describe HFM as oval vesicles on the palms and soles + oral ulcers (tongue, buccal mucosa). Enterovirus 71 HFM can cause brainstem encephalitis/severe CNS disease.

Step 1 trap
  • HFM vs HSV gingivostomatitis: both cause painful oral vesicles; HSV hits gums/lips and has no hand/foot vesicles.
  • HFM vs herpangina: herpangina (coxsackie A) = vesicles on the posterior pharynx/soft palate, no hand/foot lesions.
  • Palms/soles are also hit by secondary syphilis, RMSF and Kawasaki (edema/desquamation), but those are not vesicular.
Buzzwords
"oval vesicles on palms and soles + mouth ulcers" → HFM"daycare, summer, won't eat" → coxsackie A16"vesicular stomatitis with exanthem" → HFM

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1A child has fever, sore throat and aphthae-like erosions all over the mouth; small vesicles later appear on the hands and feet. Diagnosis and family of the cause?
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease from coxsackie A16, an enterovirus (picornavirus).
A2An infant's fever resolves and then a maculopapular rash appears. The child has no HHV-6 infection; stool PCR shows echovirus 16. What enterovirus rash pattern is this?
Roseoliform: rash begins as fever subsides, mimicking roseola (echovirus 16; coxsackie B1/B5; echo 11/25).
A3A 4-year-old has painful vesicles only on the gums and lips, with no lesions elsewhere. Why is HFM less likely?
HFM gives buccal mucosa/tongue vesicles plus hand and foot lesions. Gingiva-and-lip-only vesicles point to HSV-1 gingivostomatitis, its main look-alike.

LO 4Scarlet fever and its mimic, Kawasaki diseaseBoth give a red rash, strawberry tongue and peeling; only one needs penicillin

By the end: you can explain what causes scarlet fever, describe its rash, tongue and treatment, list the Kawasaki features and its feared complication, and tell the two apart in a vignette.
Q1. What causes scarlet fever, and what does it look like?
InfectionGroup A Streptococcus pharyngitis (or skin infection / pyoderma)
→
ToxinStrain makes a pyrogenic (erythrogenic) exotoxin
→
RashBegins 1–7 days after pharyngitis
→
RecoveryDesquamation (peeling)
  • Not viral: a bacterial toxin rash, but the textbook scarlatiniform exanthem.
  • Rash: erythematous, blanching, confluent; begins on the trunk and spreads to the extremities; spares the palms and soles.
    • “Sandpaper-like” texture (tiny 1–2 mm papules).
    • Best seen on the abdomen and in skin folds → Pastia lines (linear petechial accentuation in antecubital/axillary creases).
  • Face: circumoral pallor (flushed cheeks, pale ring around mouth).
  • Tongue: “coated” (white) tongue → strawberry tongue (red, prominent papillae).
  • Treatment: penicillin or amoxicillin.
CheckIs the scarlet fever rash caused by bacteria growing in the skin?
No. The bacteria stay in the throat (or skin wound); the rash is caused by a circulating pyrogenic exotoxin.
Step 1 HY
  • Pyrogenic exotoxins (SpeA/SpeC) are superantigens → same family of toxins behind streptococcal toxic shock.
  • Boards phrase the rash spread as starting on the neck/upper trunk and groin/axillae, then spreading to the trunk and extremities; in-house, learn trunk → extremities, sparing palms and soles.
  • Treat GAS pharyngitis to prevent acute rheumatic fever.
Memory tool

SCARLET: Sore throat, Circumoral pallor, group A strep, Rash (sandpaper), Lymphadenopathy, Erythrogenic toxin, strawberry Tongue.

Buzzwords
"sandpaper rash" → scarlet fever"Pastia lines" → scarlet fever"circumoral pallor + recent sore throat" → scarlet fever"white-coated → strawberry tongue" → scarlet fever
Q2. What is Kawasaki disease, and why does it matter so much?
  • Acute, self-limited vasculitis (medium vessels) in previously healthy young children (80% <5 y).
  • Clinical features:
    • High-grade fever (≥5 days).
    • Conjunctival injection without exudate (bilateral).
    • Oral erythema / strawberry tongue; red, cracked, bleeding lips.
    • Edema and erythema of hands and feet → later periungual desquamation of fingers and toes.
    • Polymorphous rash.
    • Cervical lymphadenopathy (can be unilateral).
  • Complications: myocarditis with coronary artery aneurysms (~20–30% of untreated patients); arthritis.
  • Labs: ↑ WBC, ↑ platelets, ↑ ESR.
  • Treatment: IVIG + aspirin.
CheckWhat test do you get once Kawasaki is diagnosed, and why?
Echocardiogram → look for coronary artery aneurysms, the complication that IVIG + aspirin aim to prevent.
Step 1 HY
  • Kawasaki = one of the few pediatric indications for aspirin despite Reye syndrome risk.
  • Leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries.
  • Look-alike: MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children) after COVID-19.
Memory tool

CRASH and burn: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue (mucositis), Hands/feet changes + burn = fever ≥5 days.

Q3. Strawberry tongue + red rash + peeling: scarlet fever or Kawasaki?
FeatureScarlet feverKawasaki disease
CauseGAS pyrogenic exotoxin (bacterial)Unknown trigger → vasculitis
ThroatPharyngitis (often exudative), positive strep testOral erythema, no exudative pharyngitis
EyesNot a featureBilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection
Lips / tongueCoated → strawberry tongue; circumoral pallorStrawberry tongue; red, cracked, bleeding lips
RashSandpaper, trunk → extremities, spares palms/soles; Pastia linesPolymorphous; edema/erythema of hands and feet
PeelingDesquamation after rashPeriungual desquamation of fingers/toes
Danger(Rheumatic fever if untreated)Coronary artery aneurysms, myocarditis
LabsRapid strep / culture positive↑ WBC, ↑ platelets, ↑ ESR
TreatmentPenicillin / amoxicillinIVIG + aspirin
CheckA child with strawberry tongue has had fever for 6 days despite 3 days of amoxicillin, plus red eyes without discharge. What now?
Antibiotic failure + ≥5 days fever + non-exudative conjunctivitis → Kawasaki disease → IVIG + aspirin and an echocardiogram.
Step 1 trap
  • Strawberry tongue alone does not diagnose scarlet fever: it is also a Kawasaki finding (and TSS).
  • “Rash + strawberry tongue + no response to antibiotics + red eyes” → Kawasaki.
  • Desquamation happens in both → use conjunctivitis, fever duration and strep testing to separate.
Buzzwords
"periungual desquamation + coronary aneurysm" → Kawasaki"conjunctival injection without exudate" → Kawasaki"↑ platelets, ↑ ESR, toddler, prolonged fever" → Kawasaki

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1Three days after an untreated strep throat, a 6-year-old has a diffuse, rough, blanching rash with circumoral pallor. What bacterial product causes the rash, and what is the treatment?
Pyrogenic (erythrogenic) exotoxin of group A strep → scarlet fever → penicillin or amoxicillin.
A2Child A: exudative pharyngitis, positive rapid strep, strawberry tongue. Child B: 6 days of fever, bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, swollen hands, strawberry tongue. Diagnoses and treatments?
A = scarlet fever → penicillin/amoxicillin. B = Kawasaki → IVIG + aspirin (to prevent coronary aneurysms).
A3A child recovering from a sandpaper rash after sore throat now has peeling skin on the fingertips. Is this a new diagnosis?
No: desquamation is the expected late phase of scarlet fever. Only reconsider Kawasaki if prolonged fever, conjunctivitis and lip changes were present.
A4In a child with a diffuse blanching rash after strep throat, what are the linear red-purple streaks in the antecubital fossa called?
Pastia lines: accentuation of the scarlet fever rash in skin folds.

LO 5Exanthems in skin of colorWhen “red” doesn't look red, read texture, lesion type, distribution and mucosa

By the end: you can explain why erythema is harder to see on darker skin and identify varicella, zoster, HFM, scarlet fever, mumps and Kawasaki on darker skin using non-color clues.
Q1. Why do exanthems look different on darker skin, and what should you look for instead?
  • More epidermal melanin masks the red of dilated vessels → erythema may look violaceous, dusky, gray-brown or hyperpigmented, or be nearly invisible.
  • So shift from “how red?” to:
    • Texture → run a hand over it (sandpaper of scarlet fever).
    • Lesion type → vesicles, crusts and papules are visible regardless of skin tone.
    • Distribution → dermatome, hands/feet/mouth, cheeks, skin folds.
    • Mucosa + other signs → Koplik spots, strawberry tongue, conjunctivitis, nodes, parotid swelling.
    • Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation may outlast the rash.
CheckWhy are the oral mucosa and tongue especially useful in darker-skinned patients?
Mucosa has little melanin, so enanthems (Koplik spots, strawberry tongue, HFM vesicles) look the same in every patient.
Q2. What are the key clues for each exanthem on darker skin?

Varicella

Vesicles and crusts at different stages (some hemorrhagic) on face and body; the red halo is faint, so count stages, not color.

Herpes zoster

Grouped vesicles/crusts in a band on one side; base looks violaceous or hyperpigmented rather than red.

Hand-foot-and-mouth

Pale/gray oval papulovesicles on hands, knees, feet, buttocks; redness subtle → rely on mouth sores + poor feeding.

Scarlet fever

Fine rough “goose-flesh” papules with little visible redness; feel the sandpaper; check Pastia lines and strawberry tongue.

Mumps

Unilateral or bilateral parotid swelling obscuring the angle of the jaw + fever and headache. Color plays no role.

Kawasaki

Periungual desquamation and strawberry tongue stay obvious; rash may be hard to see.

CheckYou can barely see any redness on a febrile child's trunk, but the skin feels like fine sandpaper and the tongue is bright red. Diagnosis?
Scarlet fever. Texture + strawberry tongue (+ Pastia lines) carry the diagnosis when the erythema is masked.
Step 1 trap

Don't rule out an exanthem because you “don't see red.” On darker skin, erythema reads as purple, gray or brown; a description of “hyperpigmented papules” can still be a measles or scarlet fever stem.

Memory tool

“Feel, Find, Look inside”: feel the texture, find the distribution/lesion stage, look inside the mouth and eyes.

Step 1 HY

Boards increasingly show rashes on darker skin. Anchor on morphology words (vesicle, crust, dermatomal, sandpaper, slapped cheek, periungual peeling) rather than “erythematous.”

ApplyLO 5 application questions

A1A 70-year-old immunocompromised patient with dark skin has a painful band of grouped vesicles and crusts on one side of the trunk; the base looks purple-brown. Diagnosis?
Herpes zoster. Dermatomal grouped vesicles; the inflamed base looks violaceous/hyperpigmented rather than red.
A2A toddler with dark skin has a few days of sore throat and poor feeding, now with small gray-white papulovesicles on the hands and knees. Diagnosis?
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackie A16). Pale oval vesicles + mouth sores; redness is subtle.
A3A febrile child with dark skin has vesicles, hemorrhagic vesicles and crusted papules on the face and trunk at the same time. Diagnosis and the key clue?
Varicella. Lesions at different stages at once (asynchrony) are visible regardless of skin tone.

IMGImage ID drillName the disease (and the cause) before you open each card.

1 · Rash after 3 days of fever, cough, red eyes
Measles (rubeola), paramyxovirus: confluent morbilliform rash that spread face → trunk.
2 · Mucosal finding in an unvaccinated child
Koplik spots (measles enanthem): blue-gray/white specks on red buccal mucosa, before the rash.
3 · Itchy lesions, febrile 5-year-old
Varicella (VZV): papules, vesicles and crusts at once = asynchronous crops.
4 · 72-year-old, burning pain first
Herpes zoster: grouped vesicles in a dermatomal band (VZV reactivation from sensory ganglia).
5 · Well 6-year-old after a mild cold
Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19): slapped cheek with circumoral pallor.
6 · Appeared the day a 4-day fever broke
Roseola (HHV-6): pale pink almond-shaped macules on neck/trunk at defervescence.
7 · 3-year-old in August, won't eat
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackie A16): oval vesicles with red rim on hand and sole.
8 · Toddler, sore throat and mouth sores
HFM on darker skin: pale papulovesicles on the hand and knee; erythema subtle.
9 · Rough rash 2 days after sore throat
Scarlet fever on darker skin (GAS pyrogenic exotoxin): fine sandpaper papules, little visible red.
10 · Fever 6 days, red eyes, no exudate
Kawasaki disease: strawberry tongue + red lips → IVIG + aspirin; echo for coronary aneurysms.
11 · Late finding, toddler after prolonged fever
Kawasaki disease: periungual desquamation (scarlet fever also peels, but Kawasaki is classically periungual).

MCQPractice questionsClick an answer to see the explanation.

Score: 0 / 0

1An unvaccinated 4-year-old returns from a trip abroad with 3 days of fever, harsh cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Exam shows tiny blue-white spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars. The next day a red maculopapular rash begins at the hairline and spreads downward. The causative agent belongs to which virus family?

B. Paramyxovirus (measles). 3 C's + Koplik spots + craniocaudal rash = measles. Togavirus (A) is rubella: milder, posterior nodes, no Koplik spots. Picornavirus (C) = coxsackie (HFM). Herpesvirus (D) = VZV/HHV-6. Parvovirus (E) = slapped cheek.

2A 14-month-old has had fever to 40.2 °C for 4 days and had a brief generalized seizure on day 2. Between fever spikes she is playful. This morning the fever resolved and a pale pink macular rash appeared on her neck and trunk. Which pathogen is most likely?

A. HHV-6 (roseola). High fever 3–4 days (± febrile seizure) then rash as the fever breaks, age 6 mo–4 y. Measles (C) rash appears during fever with 3 C's. B19 (B) gives slapped cheeks. Rubella (D) has posterior nodes and no high fever. Coxsackie A16 (E) gives oral and hand/foot vesicles.

3A 9-year-old boy with sickle cell disease presents with fatigue and pallor. Hemoglobin is 4.1 g/dL (baseline 8) and the reticulocyte count is 0.2%. His younger sister recently had bright red cheeks followed by a lacy rash on her arms. Which best explains his anemia?

C. Parvovirus B19 binds the P antigen on erythroid progenitors and halts RBC production → transient aplastic crisis in patients with short RBC survival; reticulocytes ~0. Autoimmune hemolysis (A) and splenic sequestration (B) would have a high reticulocyte count. D and E don't describe B19.

4A 26-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation, who emigrated as a child and has no vaccine records, has 2 days of low-grade fever, a faint pink rash that started on her face, tender nodes behind her ears and at the back of her neck, and pain in her finger joints. Which set of findings is her fetus at greatest risk of developing?

D. Congenital rubella (posterior nodes + facial rash + arthralgia in pregnancy). Classic: deafness, heart disease (PDA), intellectual disability (+ cataracts). A = parvovirus B19. B = congenital varicella. C = toxoplasmosis. E = congenital syphilis.

5A 3-year-old boy has had fever for 6 days that has not improved with amoxicillin. He has bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge, red cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, a polymorphous truncal rash, swollen red hands and feet and a 2-cm unilateral cervical node. Rapid strep test is negative. Platelets and ESR are elevated. Which management most directly reduces his risk of the most serious complication?

E. Kawasaki disease (CRASH and burn) → IVIG + aspirin to prevent coronary artery aneurysms (20–30% if untreated). Penicillin (A) treats scarlet fever, which would have exudative pharyngitis and a positive strep test, no conjunctivitis. It is self-limited (C), but the coronary risk demands treatment. Steroids (B) are not first line; acyclovir (D) is for HSV/VZV.

6A 71-year-old man receiving chemotherapy develops severe left ear pain, then vesicles in the left external auditory canal. Two days later he cannot close his left eye or raise the left corner of his mouth, and food tastes bland. Reactivation of a latent virus in which structure explains his findings?

A. Ramsay Hunt syndrome: VZV reactivates in the geniculate ganglion (CN VII) → ear pain, canal vesicles, ipsilateral facial palsy, taste loss. B = zoster ophthalmicus (Hutchinson sign). C = classic truncal shingles. D and E don't explain facial palsy and taste loss.

7During a campus outbreak, a 20-year-old student who received two doses of MMR in childhood develops fever, headache and painful swelling below and in front of both ears that obscures the angle of the jaw. Eight days later he has a painful, swollen right testis. This infection is also classically associated with which complication?

D. Pancreatitis: mumps (paramyxovirus) causes parotitis, epididymo-orchitis (20–30% of post-pubertal males), oophoritis, pancreatitis and CSF pleocytosis/meningoencephalitis. Two-dose MMR is only ~88% effective, so outbreaks hit vaccinated young adults. A = measles; B = B19; C = Kawasaki; E = roseola.

8A 3-year-old in daycare is brought in in August because he refuses to eat or drink. He has a low-grade fever, painful shallow ulcers on his tongue and buccal mucosa, and small oval gray-white vesicles with a red rim on his palms and soles. Which best describes the causative virus?

C. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease → coxsackievirus A16, an enterovirus (naked +ssRNA picornavirus); children <10, summer/fall. B (HSV-1) causes gingivostomatitis without hand/foot vesicles. A = measles/mumps, D = rubella, E = B19.

9A 28-year-old man presents with 4 days of burning pain over the left side of his chest, followed by grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a band from his spine to the midline of his chest. He takes no medications and has no known medical problems. Which is the most appropriate additional test?

B. Dermatomal zoster is mostly a disease of the elderly and immunocompromised; in a young adult it should prompt evaluation for immunosuppression, especially HIV. A = GAS sequelae, C = Kawasaki, D = mumps pancreatitis, E = B19.

10A 5-year-old with chickenpox has crops of macules, papules, vesicles and crusts on the trunk. On day 4 one excoriated lesion on his thigh becomes the center of an expanding, warm, tender, red plaque, and he spikes a fever to 39.8 °C. Which organism is the most likely cause of this new problem?

E. Group A strep (with S. aureus) superinfects varicella lesions → cellulitis, impetigo, invasive GAS. Pseudomonas (A) = hot tubs/thermal wounds, Pasteurella (B) = animal bites, Hib (C) = unvaccinated cellulitis/epiglottitis, Candida (D) = moist intertriginous skin.

11A 6-year-old had a sore throat with tonsillar exudate 3 days ago. Now she has a diffuse, blanching, rough rash that began on her trunk and spread to her limbs, sparing her palms and soles, with accentuation in the antecubital creases, flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor and a red tongue with prominent papillae. Which bacterial product is directly responsible for the rash?

D. Scarlet fever is caused by GAS pyrogenic exotoxin (a superantigen): sandpaper rash, Pastia lines, circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue; treat with penicillin/amoxicillin. Streptolysin O (A) lyses RBCs (ASO titer). M protein (B) is antiphagocytic (rheumatic fever mimicry). Capsule (C) resists phagocytosis. Streptokinase (E) activates plasminogen.

12A 34-year-old kindergarten teacher develops symmetric pain and swelling of the small joints of both hands, wrists and feet. Two weeks earlier several children in her class had bright red cheeks with pale skin around the mouth. Which describes the genome of the most likely causative virus?

C. Parvovirus B19 (ssDNA, naked) → slapped cheek in kids, symmetric small-joint arthropathy in adults (mimics early RA). A = herpesviruses, B = rubella/picornaviruses, D = measles/mumps, E = rotavirus.

13An unvaccinated 6-year-old's measles rash appeared on Friday. Public health asks which classmates were exposed. His unvaccinated classmates were last with him on Monday of the same week. Which statement is correct?

A. Measles is contagious 5 days before through 4 days after the exanthem; Monday is 4 days before Friday. It spreads by respiratory droplets/airborne (not lesions, C/D) and the attack rate in susceptible hosts is ~90% (E).
